title: Transfer Learning for Credit Card Fraud Detection: A Journey from Research to Production
abstract: The dark face of digital commerce generalization is the increase of fraud attempts. To prevent any type of attacks, state-of-the-art fraud detection systems are now embedding Machine Learning (ML) modules. The conception of such modules is only communicated at the level of research and papers mostly focus on results for isolated benchmark datasets and metrics. But research is only a part of the journey, preceded by the right formulation of the business problem and collection of data, and followed by a practical integration. In this paper, we give a wider vision of the process, on a case study of transfer learning for fraud detection, from business to research, and back to business.

title: Learning Transactional Behavioral Representations for Credit Card Fraud Detection
venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
abstract: Credit card fraud detection is a challenging task since fraudulent actions are hidden in massive legitimate behaviors. This work aims to learn a new representation for each transaction record based on the historical transactions of users in order to capture fraudulent patterns accurately and, thus, automatically detect a fraudulent transaction. We propose a novel model by improving long short-term memory with a time-aware gate that can capture the behavioral changes caused by consecutive transactions of users. A current-historical attention module is designed to build up connections between current and historical transactional behaviors, which enables the model to capture behavioral periodicity. An interaction module is designed to learn comprehensive and rational behavioral representations. To validate the effectiveness of the learned behavioral representations, experiments are conducted on a large real-world transaction dataset provided to us by a financial company in China, as well as a public dataset. title: FraudGNN-RL: A Graph Neural Network With Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Financial Fraud Detection

abstract: As financial systems become increasingly complex and interconnected, traditional fraud detection methods struggle to keep pace with sophisticated fraudulent activities. This article introduces FraudGNN-RL, an innovative framework that combines Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with Reinforcement Learning (RL) for adaptive and context-aware financial fraud detection. Our approach models financial transactions as a dynamic graph, where entities (e.g., users, merchants) are nodes and transactions form edges. We propose a novel GNN architecture, Temporal-Spatial-Semantic Graph Convolution (TSSGC), which simultaneously captures temporal patterns, spatial relationships, and semantic information in transaction data. The RL component, implemented as a Deep Q-Network (DQN), dynamically adjusts the fraud detection threshold and feature importance, allowing the model to adapt to evolving fraud patterns and minimize detection costs. We further introduce a Federated Learning scheme to enable collaborative model training across multiple financial institutions while preserving data privacy. As well known, money laundering (ML) is critical to the effective operation of transnational and organized crime, which affects a country's economy, government, and social wellbeings. Financial services organizations facilitate the movement of money and have been enlisted by governments to assist with the detection and prevention of money laundering, which is a key tool in the fight to reduce crime and create sustainable economic development. In the application of AML, user identity and financial behavior data are widely used to detect laundering transactions. In recent years, an increasing number of money laundering activities have been conducted by organized criminal gangs while most existing works still treat the actions of each account as independent identity behavior without considering the group-level conspired interactions. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a group-aware deep graph learning-based approach for organized money-laundering detection. title: Tainted Love: a Systematic Literature Review of Online Romance Scam Research
abstract: Abstract Romance scams involve cybercriminals engineering a romantic relationship on online dating platforms for monetary gain. It is a cruel form of cybercrime whereby victims are left heartbroken, often facing financial ruin. We characterize the literary landscape on romance scams, advancing the understanding of researchers and practitioners by systematically reviewing and synthesizing contemporary qualitative and quantitative evidence. The systematic review establishes influencing factors of victimhood and explores countermeasures for mitigating romance scams. We searched 10 scholarly databases and websites using terms related to romance scams. The methodology followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) guidelines: a total of 279 papers were screened. One hundred seven papers were assessed for eligibility, and 53 were included in the final analysis. title: ASA-GNN: Adaptive Sampling and Aggregation-Based Graph Neural Network for Transaction Fraud Detection
venue: IEEE Transactions on Computational Social Systems
abstract: Many machine learning methods have been proposed to achieve accurate transaction fraud detection, which is essential to the financial security of individuals and banks. However, most existing methods either leverage original features only or require manual feature engineering so that they show a weak ability to learn discriminative representations from transaction data. Moreover, criminals often commit fraud by imitating cardholders’; behaviors, which causes the poor performance of existing detection models. In this article, we propose an adaptive sampling and aggregation-based graph neural network (ASA-GNN) that learns discriminative representations to improve the performance of transaction fraud detection. A neighbor sampling strategy is performed to filter noisy nodes and supplement information for fraudulent nodes. Specifically, we use cosine similarity and edge weights to adaptively select neighbors with similar behavior patterns for target nodes and then find multihop neighbors for fraudulent nodes. A neighbor diversity metric is designed by calculating the entropy of neighbors to tackle the camouflage issue of fraudsters and explicitly alleviate the oversmoothing phenomena.

title: LGM-GNN: A Local and Global Aware Memory-Based Graph Neural Network for Fraud Detection
abstract: Graphs have been widely adopted to accomplish fraud detection tasks because of their inherently favorable structure to capture the intricate features in many complicated scenarios, especially in some modern e-commerce situations that have various relation attributes like transactions. These works tend to utilize the direct aggregate information about neighbor nodes of the target node or the aggregation of the neighbor information after the conditional filter and mostly use local information but ignore global information. However, in some cases, local abnormal points are detected in the global view, so global information is very important for fraud detection. In this article, we propose a local and global aware memory-based graph neural network for fraud detection (LGM-GNN). It first obtains the preliminary node embedding through relation-aware embedding and then interactively aggregates the local and global memory network to fuse and utilize the local and global information. title: Dual Defense: Adversarial, Traceable, and Invisible Robust Watermarking Against Face Swapping
venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
abstract: Malicious applications of deep face swapping technology pose security threats such as misinformation dissemination and identity fraud. Some research propose the utilization of robust watermarking methods to track the copyright of facial images, facilitating post-forgery identity attribution. However, these methods cannot fundamentally prevent or eliminate the adverse impacts of face swapping. To address this issue, we present Dual Defense, an innovative framework based on robust adversarial watermarking. It simultaneously tracks image copyrights and disrupts the face swapping model by one-time embedding the robust adversarial watermark. Specifically, we propose an Original-domain Feature Emulation Attack (OFEA) method, which makes the traceable watermark adversarial through specially designed original domain adversarial loss. title: Economic crime, economic criminology, and serious crimes for economic gain: On the conceptual and disciplinary (dis)order of the object of study
abstract: This article has two main objectives. First, to interrogate the concept and/or conception of ‘economic crime’ (framed as a singular thing). We argue that current policy, and subsequently, social scientific (or criminological more specifically) framings, tend to arbitrarily ‘carve up’ the objects of study that interest us, in turn creating a ‘conceptual disorder’ that has implications for how we explain, and respond to, these harmful crimes. This raises questions about the value of the concept of ‘economic crime’ and about the related process of conceptual abstraction. In analytical terms, we argue that more can be gained by focusing on the necessary and contingent relations of serious crimes for economic gain. Second, to scrutinise the logic of ‘economic criminology’ (framed in terms of a singular discipline) and assess the value that criminology can add to analyses of related behaviours. title: Cybercriminal networks in the UK and Beyond: Network structure, criminal cooperation and external interactions
abstract: Abstract This article examines the network structure, criminal cooperation, and external interactions of cybercriminal networks. Its contribution is empirical and inductive. The core of this study involved carrying out 10 case analyses on closed cybercrime investigations – all with financial motivations on the part of the offenders - in the UK and beyond. Each analysis involved investigator interview and access to unpublished law enforcement files. The comparison of these cases resulted in a wide range of findings on these cybercriminal networks, including: a common division between the scam/attack components and the money components; the presence of offline/local elements; a broad, and sometimes blurred, spectrum of cybercriminal behaviour and organisation. An overarching theme across the cases that we observe is that cybercriminal business models are relatively stable.

title: Romance baiting, cryptorom and ‘pig butchering’: an evolutionary step in romance fraud
abstract: Romance fraud uses the guise of a genuine relationship to deceive a victim into transferring often large amounts of money to an offender/s.Romance fraud has been in the top three categories of financial loss for Australian victims over the past decade, and this is a trend mirrored internationally.However, in recent years there has been a convergence of romance fraud and investment fraud approaches.Terms such as romance baiting, cryptorom and 'pig butchering' have all emerged to describe how offenders are evolving in their attempts to defraud victims through offering fake cryptocurrency investment opportunities, using a relationship as the mechanism.This article analyses this shift in romance fraud offending and its embracing of investment scheme opportunities.It highlights the underlying reasons for the success of this amalgamated approach and further demonstrates how it potentially distorts the reporting of fraud as well as prevention messaging targeting these incidents.

title: Fraud as Legitimate Retribution for Colonial Injustice: Neutralization Techniques in Interviews with Police and Online Romance Fraud Offenders
abstract: This qualitative research examines the phenomenon of online romance fraud, exploring it from contrasting perspectives. The study engaged two distinct groups of participants: (1) fraudsters actively involved in online romance scams (commonly referred to as “Sakawa Boys”) and (2) police officers with experience in investigating and policing internet crimes. We explore the usefulness of neutralization techniques in interpreting data within the cultural context of individuals’ subjective experiences. Thematic analysis of data reveals that both offenders and police officers employ certain neutralization techniques, such as denial of responsibility, condemnation of the condemners, and appeals to higher loyalties, to justify their conduct. In particular, online romance offenders invoke higher loyalties, rationalizing their actions as reparative justice for colonial exploitation and framing their fraud as a means of reclaiming wealth unjustly taken during colonial rule. title: Network Analytics for Anti-money Laundering—A Systematic Literature Review and Experimental Evaluation
abstract: Money laundering presents a pervasive challenge, burdening society by financing illegal activities. The use of network information is increasingly being explored to effectively combat money laundering given that it involves connected parties. This led to a surge in research on network analytics for anti-money laundering (AML). The literature is, however, fragmented, and a comprehensive overview of existing work is missing. This results in limited understanding of the methods to apply and their comparative detection power. This paper presents an extensive and unique literature review based on 97 papers from Web of Science and Scopus, resulting in a taxonomy following a recently proposed fraud analytics framework. We conclude that most research relies on expert-based rules and manual features, whereas deep learning methods have been gaining traction. title: Blockchain Address Poisoning
abstract: In many blockchains, e.g., Ethereum, Binance Smart Chain (BSC), the primary representation used for wallet addresses is a hardly memorable 40-digit hexadecimal string. As a result, users often select addresses from their recent transaction history, which enables blockchain address poisoning. The adversary first generates lookalike addresses similar to one with which the victim has previously interacted, and then engages with the victim to ``poison'' their transaction history. The goal is to have the victim mistakenly send tokens to the lookalike address, as opposed to the intended recipient. Compared to contemporary studies, this paper provides four notable contributions. title: TREASURE: The Visa Payment Foundation Model for High-Volume Transaction Understanding
abstract: Payment networks form the backbone of modern commerce, generating high volumes of transaction records from daily activities. Properly modeling this data can enable applications such as abnormal behavior detection and consumer-level insights for hyper-personalized experiences, ultimately improving people's lives. In this paper, we present TREASURE, TRansformer Engine As Scalable Universal transaction Representation Encoder, a multipurpose transformer-based foundation model specifically designed for transaction data. The model simultaneously captures both consumer behavior and payment network signals (such as response codes and system flags), providing comprehensive information necessary for applications like accurate recommendation systems and abnormal behavior detection. Verified with industry-grade datasets, TREASURE features three key capabilities: 1) an input module with dedicated sub-modules for static and dynamic attributes, enabling more efficient training and inference; 2) an efficient and effective training paradigm for predicting high-cardinality categorical attributes; and 3) demonstrated effectiveness as both a standalone model that increases abnormal behavior detection

title: PersonaAgent: Retrieval-Augmented Transaction Anomaly Scoring with Refreshable Multi-Entity Persona Memory
abstract: In large-scale payment networks, entities (card, merchant, etc.) and their interactions play a key role in transaction anomaly detection. However, transaction patterns between different entities usually change more frequently than the production model refresh schedule. Meanwhile, entity embedding tables suffer from high-cardinality and sparse interaction issues. To resolve the above challenges, we present PersonaAgent, an agentic transaction anomaly detection framework which represents the latest entity behavior signals as personas and saves them in a refreshable memory. Offline, a weekly scheduled batch job is used to extract the latest behavior signals and update them in the memory. At inference time, a lightweight adapter retrieves the corresponding entity behavior signals of each transaction from memory and uses them to augment the base anomaly classifier's scoring. Through comprehensive benchmarking with different anomaly detection models at Visa, PersonaAgent is able to score transactions efficiently (a 1,000-transaction CPU batch in 1-2 ms), lifting the PR-AUC by 0.65-6.58% and the production business metric by 8.93-14.24% relatively in deployment.

title: Financial stability implications of AI adoption in the financial industry and the real economy
abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the financial industry as well as the broader economy, creating both opportunities and risks. Banks and asset managers, which represent key channels of financial intermediation in the euro area, are increasingly using AI for tasks such as credit scoring, fraud detection and portfolio management. While AI adoption can support innovation and enhance operational efficiency, it may also introduce new risks and amplify existing vulnerabilities, including a reliance on a small number of technology providers that creates concentration and third-party dependencies across the financial system. At the same time, financial institutions are also increasingly exposed to AI-driven developments in the real economy. A novel firm-level indicator suggests that a sizeable share of firms, concentrated mainly in the IT and financial sectors, is significantly exposed to AI-related opportunities and risks. Policies should focus on improving the quality of data that monitor the use of AI, strengthening the oversight of critical AI providers and adapting market safeguards and supervisory capabilities to emerging risks.

title: Generative AI and the restructuring of criminal opportunity
abstract: Fifty years after Crime as Opportunity (Mayhew et al., 1976 ), the opportunity paradigm remains criminology’s most productive account of how and where crime happens. This theoretical article asks what generative artificial intelligence (hereafter AI) does to the opportunity structure that the paradigm describes. It argues that AI is not merely another item in the long list of technologies that create new targets; it is a change in the supply of offender capability itself. AI lowers the effort required to offend, weakens the perceived risk of detection and raises the expected yield per attempt, moving previously unprofitable targets across the threshold of viability. title: A systematic review of transparent artificial intelligence models for credit card fraud detection
abstract: Research on credit card fraud detection has rapidly increased over the past decade due to the increasing use of digital payments and the financial losses caused by fraud. Despite extensive research, most studies focus on detection performance, while transparency, fairness, and auditability remain under-studied, although they matter under regimes such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and, for credit-scoring uses of fraud scores, the EU AI Act. This review argues that accountability, the ability to explain, audit, and demonstrate fairness in automated decisions, is under-explored compared to detection performance, and performance-related limits (imbalance handling, generalization, and offline-only testing) also remain unaddressed. title: Coerced but “Authorised”: Allocating Loss in India's Digital Arrest Frauds and the Case for a Statutory Reimbursement Regime
venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
abstract: In a “digital arrest” fraud, callers posing as police, customs or central-agency officers convince a victim over video that she is under investigation and must move her savings into a “verification” account to avoid arrest. The victim makes the transfers herself. That single fact has shaped how Indian law allocates the loss. abstract: Financial fraud is increasingly coordinated across multiple accounts and transactions, meaning that its evidence often lies in relationships between accounts, the sequence of events, and, in schemes such as money laundering and wash trading, closed loops of transfers rather than in individual records. This review examines graph-based methods for detecting such fraud, covering static and temporal graph neural networks, graph anomaly detection, cycle- and motif-aware methods, generative models, and the evaluation practices used to assess them. title: Early Detection of Financial Crime Risks: A Conceptual Framework for Incorporating Heuristic Decision Rules into Suspicious Activity Reporting
abstract: This conceptual article advances anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT) research by proposing a novel, explainable framework for embedding simple heuristic decision rules into internal suspicious transaction reporting (STR) and suspicious activity reporting (SAR) workflows. Existing transaction-monitoring tools often suffer from massive false-positive burdens (frequently exceeding 90–95%) and operate primarily ex post, struggling to provide timely pre-execution risk indicators. title: Generative AI and Agentic AI in Financial Crimes Compliance

abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) (GenAI) (e.g. large language models) and agentic AI (autonomous, goal directed AI agents) offer powerful new capabilities for financial-crime compliance, including Anti Money Laundering (“AML”)/Combating Finance of Terrorism (“CFT”) programs, customer due diligence, transaction monitoring, and investigations. These technologies can automate and scale tasks such as Suspicious Activity Report(“SAR”) narrative drafting, alert triage, and data analysis, potentially improving detection rates and freeing human analysts for complex work. However, they introduce novel risks - for example, “confabulation” (AI-generated false or misleading content), privacy and bias issues, and loss of human control over automated processes. abstract: Abstract Liability for scam losses is shifting towards banks, yet few interpretable tools can anticipate which fraud and scam complaints will end in redress. abstract: In financial risk control, banks need to share fraud-detection capability, but privacy rules make raw transaction sharing difficult. Federated Learning (FL) is often used to handle this conflict. Under the common Federated Averaging (FedAvg) setting, however, poisoned updates can still enter the global model, because the server averages client gradients with little quality check. This paper builds a dynamic FL setup with a decentralized reputation incentive, and puts a Reputation-FedAvg strategy at its center. Before aggregation, the server checks each client’s update on a separate validation set. Clients that help the model get higher reputation and larger aggregation weights; clients that hurt the model lose score step by step and may be removed. The method is tested in the Flower simulator on a highly imbalanced credit card fraud dataset. Under strong label-flipping attacks, Reputation-FedAvg raises the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) by 5.7% over attacked FedAvg, and Recall reaches 0.8571. The reputation tracker also finds and isolates Byzantine clients with no false-positive removals. These results support its use in cross-bank financial FL systems.

This paper introduces an end-to-end VoiceShield system which classifies speech as real or fake for five Indian languages (Hindi, Marathi, Urdu, Kannada and Bengali) using a single multilingual classifier. Audio is standardized to 16 kHz mono, segmented in 4-s chunks with 2-s hop, and transformed to 128-band spectrograms on a log Mel scale, and classified using a compact, 0.39 million parameter convolutional neural network (CNN). By recording-level stratified splitting, leakage of segments does not occur, and by using the Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), the time–frequency regions responsible for each decision can be highlighted. The trained network is exported to TorchScript and served using a FastAPI back end which has 2 modes: file upload with per-segment analysis, and WebSocket based real-time monitoring, and a React front end. title: VRLLM: Turning LLMs into Powerful Tabular Classifiers
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on text, but whether pretrained LLMs are effective for large-scale tabular classification remains unclear, as many previous works demonstrate that LLMs' tabular data classification performance falls behind tree-based models or neural architectures designed for tabular data. At Visa Research, we managed to fine-tune a pretrained Llama 3.2 1B LLM on billions of rows of labeled tabular data and make it outperform a wide array of tabular classifiers and even our competitive production deep learning model. For ease of reference, we refer to the model as the Visa Research LLM (VRLLM). In this paper, we share how we achieved this exciting result, covering data preparation, training recipe, ablation studies of design choices and deployment validation. We also benchmark frontier LLMs on the same task and analyze their prediction behavior across model families and generations. abstract: Abstract Research on inter-bank fraud detection in Nigeria is limited by the lack of shareable transaction data, and synthetic benchmarks can mislead if they leak information or hide their assumptions. FraudBench-NG is a reproducible framework for studying fraud detection under explicitly documented modelling assumptions. It is a parametric simulation calibrated to 2023 NIBSS aggregates, with a released dataset of 2.1~million transactions from 25{,}000 customers and 0.1\% fraud. Fraud is generated as incidents, matching NIBSS counts and loss per case; every parameter is marked as NIBSS or assumed; and every behavioural feature uses only prior transactions, verified by row-by-row recomputation and a label-permutation test. Logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost reach a PR-AUC of 0.016--0.036 (no-skill 0.0007), with wide customer-level bootstrap intervals, so the models cannot be ranked. At a 1\% false-positive rate they raise about 70 false alerts per fraud row caught and flag only about 19\% of incidents at their first transaction. title: Communication Abuse: Why Spam and Scam Calls, Texts and Emails Persist — and What It Would Take to Stop Them
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Scam and spam calls, texts, emails and ads, which this paper calls communication abuse, drive much of the 15.9 billion dollars in fraud losses Americans reported to federal authorities in 2025. That figure is nearly five times the 2020 total. Because most victims never report, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) estimates the true cost could be as high as 195.9 billion dollars. The paper asks why the problem persists despite decades of laws, fines and blocking tools. Its core finding is that enforcement targets scam callers, who are mostly overseas and almost never pay. Meanwhile, the carriers, platforms and payment companies that carry the traffic are paid on volume and face little liability. Courts have narrowed the 1991 Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA), Congress has not updated it, and no single agency owns the problem from first contact to stolen dollar. The abuse has also moved to social media, messaging and dating apps, and political texting, where the rules are weakest. It now runs on bot farms, dark-web phishing kits, forced-labor scam compounds and AI voice cloning. Older adults and people with disabilities lose the most per person and get the least help recovering.

title: JEV vs. LLMs: A Comparative Analysis for Phishing Email Detection
abstract: Phishing remains a major source of credential theft and fraudulent payments, and email security systems must classify large message volumes reliably, quickly, and at manageable cost. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer flexible text understanding, but their token-based generation increases response time and API cost, and the reliability of their confidence values requires measurement. Jev 1.13, a typed decision model from TypeSafe AI, instead returns a structured outcome with a confidence value. This paper compares Jev 1.13 with Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra, and Meta Llama 4 Maverick on a labelled dataset of 1500 emails, covering classification performance, decision latency, token consumption, API cost, and probability calibration. Jev achieves the highest accuracy (79.67%), precision (71.43%), recall (97.97%), and F1 score (82.62%). It also records the shortest batch time (173.88 seconds), the lowest token count (597,895), the lowest cost (USD 0.015103 per 1000 decisions), and the lowest Brier score (0.1698) and ECE (0.1594). title: "I Don't Think It's a Scam": A First Look at Family Intervention Barriers in Elder Abuse Discussions on Reddit and Baidu Tieba
abstract: When older adults trust scammers despite warnings, families face obstacles to intervention. Complainants aged 60 and older reported \$4.9 billion in losses in 2024 to the U.S. Internet Crime Complaint Center. To investigate family intervention barriers to elder scams, we collected 2M Reddit posts from May 2021 to June 2026 and 2B Baidu Tieba posts from 2007 to 2026. The final corpora contain 13,082 Reddit posts and 3,933 Baidu Tieba posts, labeled using platform-specific codebooks, manual reference annotations, and LLM coding. Through a mixed-methods analysis, we find that scams often extend beyond a single incident and are reported alongside debt problems and broken family relationships. In 68.0\% of Reddit posts recording reactions, older adults showed resistance or continued involvement; in Baidu Tieba family-confrontation posts, 41.9\% showed continued belief. Relatives identified fraud in 74.4\% of Reddit posts and narrated cases on Baidu Tieba, but without the victim's consent, relatives may lack the legal authority to intervene. title: Reassessing Unsupervised Anomaly Augmentation for Fraud Detection: The Roles of Distribution Shift, Learner Instability, and Run-to-Run Variability
abstract: Unsupervised anomaly scores are often added to supervised fraud classifiers, but an apparent gain may stem from learner instability or from the mere addition of a column rather than from anomaly information. We propose a controlled evaluation protocol that combines temporal splitting, multi-seed replication, uninformative negative-control columns, learner-stability checks and prespecified equivalence margins. It is applied to LightGBM and XGBoost with six anomaly representations on the Bank Account Fraud (BAF) benchmark and the chronologically split CreditCard dataset, including rolling-origin windows. On BAF, a single-seed gain of 3.5% in mean-variant AUPRC shrank to 1.2% under multi-seed evaluation, matching the 1.1% gain of a random-noise column. On CreditCard, changing only the LightGBM bagging seed moved baseline AUPRC between 0.004 and 0.742. title: RUID: Privacy-preserving multi-factor authentication through ephemeral user identifiers
abstract: This paper introduces RUID (Random User Identifier and Dynamic), a privacy-preserving multi-factor authentication (MFA) protocol. Traditional MFA and federated identity frameworks rely on static user identifiers, leaving them vulnerable to user enumeration, cross-session tracking, and credential stuffing. RUID mitigates these threats by replacing persistent identifiers with ephemeral, single-use identifiers cryptographically bound to a registered client device. By removing the static identity from the network transit phase, RUID prevents early-stage reconnaissance and identity correlation. The protocol is analysed using a five-stage approach which provides a precise monitor of the security and performance limits of the extensively used authentication mechanisms. The protocol is assessed against the prominent authentication framework like OAuth2+OIDC, SAML2 based federation, smart card based schemes and digital signature based approaches. The protocol is analysed as benchmark, measuring success rates of attacks, authentication latency, and failure behavior in adverse conditions. venue: International Journal of World Economic Research
abstract: Fraud-screening labels often arrive after a transaction, with fraudulent outcomes confirmed later than legitimate outcomes. This class-dependent observation process distorts conventional replay under concept drift. We instantiate the adaptive recent/global prioritized replay of DriftShield in a one-step cost-sensitive fraud controller, and extend it with maturity-gated access, transaction-time recency and capped inverse confirmation-visibility weighting. A second, arrival-driven scorer supplies a faster adaptation channel; its predictions are combined with the slow replay scorer using a fixed mixture. The system is tested prequentially on an explicitly synthetic 42,000-event stream with two changes in fraud signatures and asymmetric reporting delays. In the three-seed comparison, 42 model/delay runs include three component ablations and two stress-test delays. An additional 12-seed paired evaluation reports F1 0.262 and average precision 0.236 for the dual-timescale controller, versus 0.239 and 0.223 for arrival-time replay. venue: Journal of theoretical and applied electronic commerce research
abstract: Management information systems (MISs) are subject to complex patterns of fraud, which change over time, as they occur at high speeds in class-imbalanced data streams. E-commerce platforms process very large transaction volumes. Existing detectors have three structural problems. The quadratic complexity of transformer attention makes it difficult to meet millisecond-scale inference budgets, recurrent models suffer from gradient pathologies over long behavioral sequences, and static loss functions are unable to adjust to the severe and changing class imbalance found in real transaction logs. This article introduces a selective state-space framework (SHOPMAMBA-MIS) that tackles all three challenges within a single framework. abstract: Coordinated fraud can produce repeated, synchronized transfers whose signatures are obscured by heterogeneous activity, missing edges, and evolving behavior. Three independent runs use chronological, nonoverlapping train/validation/test snapshots. title: DOiT: Better Money-Flow Ranking Can Coexist with Worse Account Selection in Anti-Money Laundering Review
abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) review selects suspicious accounts and reconstructs transfers. Downstream graph neural networks (GNNs) rank money-flow evidence but may also reorder the account queue. DOiT separates these decisions at equal review capacity: account selection determines where graph investigation starts. Across AMLWorld and AMLNet, GNN reordering harms higher-yield upstream orders but helps lower-yield ones. On AMLWorld, this harm coexists with higher transaction average precision (AP) in dimension-matched, per-run decoders, demonstrating separable ranking abilities. At small capacities, positive neighbors can displace a denser upstream prefix and lower yield; replacement costs fall as that prefix is exhausted, allowing the preferred order to reverse. A restricted-access synthetic benchmark informed by real transaction patterns reproduces this separation and validation-based upstream preservation. Capacity-matched combination protects upstream ordering while retaining GNN money-flow analysis, admitting GNN queue influence only where held-out evidence supports it.

title: JevRisk: Zero-Shot Financial Risk Assessment with a Language Decision Model
abstract: Banks must monitor every customer's financial risk, such as money laundering and credit default, by interpreting financial activity in the context of the customer's profile. Existing risk monitoring systems of banks are mostly based on expert-designed risk indicators, which apply predefined thresholds to every customer and cannot adapt to their personal situations. Supervised models recognise risk patterns from labelled customers, but each label often needs an expert's review or months of repayment history, which is slow and costly. Financial risk assessment therefore calls for a zero-shot decision system that minimises the need for labels and generalises across customers and risk types. To this end, we present JevRisk, a system for zero-shot financial risk assessment with a language decision model. JevRisk works in two steps. First, following regulatory guidelines in the finance domain, JevRisk computes exact risk indicators with code. abstract: In finance, fraud detection systems frequently struggle to balance accurate predictions with fair outcomes. Many of the machine learning models used today are black boxes, and may be biased based on the data they were trained on, resulting in unfair results. abstract: Smishing is a cyberattack in which fraudulent Short Message Service (SMS) messages are used to obtain personal or financial information by deceiving users. For a Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT), identifying the smishing type (bank/financial, delivery, or e-commerce) helps determine the impersonated entity. However, existing datasets are English-centric, leaving other languages underexplored. We present a controlled benchmark to study automatic translation on multi-class smishing classification, along two complementary lines: multilingual classification and back-translation augmentation for English. We introduce MIMICS-3500-16L, comprising 3500 seven-class smishing messages translated into 15 languages, and MIMICS-56000-BT, containing 56,000 original and back-translated variants. We present four experiments: (1) evaluation of multilingual models (XLM-RoBERTa, mBERT) on 16 languages, (2) comparison of six embeddings (TweetEval, FastText, USE, SMS-Bert, SentenceBert, RoBERTa) as input for SVM, LR, RF, and XGB, (3) proposal for fusion of embeddings, and (4) evaluation of back-translated sample selection using ROUGE and METEOR. abstract: Behavioral continuous authentication can update a user’s profile during operation, but accepted-only adaptation links access errors to future model states. abstract: Voice cloning now needs only seconds of audio, and detectors tuned to one dataset often fail when the generator, channel, or language changes. We introduce ARCAS 290M, Neural Defend's foundation model for detecting AI-generated audio. A single frozen production model, with no benchmark-specific fine-tuning, generalizes across text-to-speech, voice-conversion, and codec-language-model generators, telephone and Bluetooth channels, recording conditions, and languages. ARCAS 290M ranks first among all systems on the Podonos leaderboard and has the lowest equal error rate among commercial detectors on ASVspoof5. abstract: Two public benchmarks dominate graph-based anti-money-laundering (AML) research on Bitcoin: the transaction-level Elliptic dataset, extended as Elliptic++, and the subgraph-level Elliptic2. abstract: This paper addresses human-in-the-loop compliance automation for obliged entities when the anti-money laundering legal corpus is amended. abstract: Online fraud is traditionally limited by the cost of the human labor needed to talk to potential victims. We ask whether hosted large language models will now supply that labor. abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. abstract: A growing concern in consumer financial applications is the necessity of protection in the face of challenging, dynamic cyber threats. This is primarily attributed to interaction networks between users and devices becoming high dimensional and imbalanced. The classic models of securing a computer system have proven to be inadequate to describe the complex relationships of coordinated attacks, and the evolving strategies of threat actors are incompatible with static graph approaches.
